references.text: Luke 18:7 deals with God's righteous judgment and vengeance for His chosen ones. Several central themes intersect here: God's ekdikesis (vengeance/justice), His elect (eklektoi), their persistent cry day and night, and God's patience.

[ref:Deut 32:35|Deuteronomy 32:35] – "Vengeance is mine, I will repay." God's promise to take vengeance for His people is the basis for the expectation that He will secure justice for His chosen ones.
[ref:Ps 22:2-3|Psalms 22:2-3] – The cry to God day and night without receiving an answer reflects the believers' persistent prayer in Luke 18:7, where they call out to Him day and night.
[ref:Exod 22:22-23|Exodus 22:22-23] – God promises to hear the cry of the oppressed and secure justice for them. This supports the principle that God answers those who cry out to Him in distress.
[ref:Ps 88:2|Psalms 88:2] – "O Lord, my God of salvation, I cry out day and night before you." The expression "day and night" for persistent prayer to God is a recurring theme in the Psalms.

[ref:Isa 62:6-7|Isaiah 62:6-7] – The watchmen on Jerusalem's walls shall never be silent, day or night, and give the Lord no rest until He fulfills His promises. A close parallel image to the elect who cry out to God day and night.
[ref:Isa 65:9|Isaiah 65:9] – God's chosen ones are explicitly mentioned as heirs of His promises. The term "eklektoi" (chosen) has roots in the Old Testament concept of Israel's election.

[ref:Rev 6:10|Revelation 6:10] – The souls of the martyrs under the altar cry out: "O Lord, holy and true, how long before you judge and avenge our blood?" A strong parallel to the cry for God's righteous vengeance in Luke 18:7.
[ref:Rom 8:33|Romans 8:33] – "Who will bring any charge against God's chosen ones?" Paul uses the same term "eklektoi" (chosen) and assures that God is the one who justifies them.

[ref:2 Pet 3:9|2 Peter 3:9] – The Lord is patient (makrothymei) and desires all to come to repentance. The same Greek verb for patience is used as in Luke 18:7, illuminating why God seemingly delays intervening.

[ref:Jas 5:7-8|James 5:7-8] – James encourages patience while waiting for the Lord's coming and uses the term makrothymia (patience), linking it to God's patience and the believers' perseverance in prayer.

[ref:Ps 9:13|Psalms 9:13] – "For He who requires blood remembers them; He does not forget the cry of the afflicted." God does not forget those who cry out to Him, which underscores the promise in Luke 18:7.

[ref:Sir 35:22|Sirach 35:22] is not canonical, but [ref:Hab 2:3|Habakkuk 2:3] says: "For the vision awaits an appointed time ... if it seems to tarry, wait for it; it will surely come, it will not delay." This supports the theme that God's righteous intervention is certain, even if it delays.

[ref:Hab 2:3|Habakkuk 2:3] – The vision awaits an appointed time, and though it seems to tarry, it will not fail. The parallel to Luke 18:7 is clear: God will secure justice, even if He appears to delay.

[ref:Luke 18:1|Luke 18:1] – The context of the parable: Jesus told it to show that they should always pray and not lose heart. Verse 7 is the answer to this – God will certainly secure justice for His chosen ones.
